docs.title: TorBots Docs
docs.text:
Team-wide documentation for FRC Team 1197 TorBots: how the team works, how we design and build robots today, and the record of each season.

This site is separate from the per-project documentation that ships with our software:

  • ScouTor docs — scouting system
  • TorKit docs — engineering analysis toolkit

docs.title: How this site is organized
docs.text:
• Team, Mechanical, Electrical, and Programming describe how we do things today. The subteam standards hold every rule we've learned, with the reason and the season it came from. When a new lesson changes a rule, the rule is updated in place.
  • Seasons is the record. Each season's plan and retros live there, and each lesson links to the standard it changed. You never need to read through past seasons to find the current answer.

docs.title: Standards
docs.text:
How we design and build robots today. Each standard lists why we do it and which season taught us.

  • Power Transmission: belts, pulleys, shafts, hubs, and ratios
  • Structure & Materials: plate, pocketing, robot width, standoffs, friction, polycarb
  • Bearings & Retention: retaining and aligning bearings
  • Linear Motion: constraining anything that slides or extends
  • Intakes: compliant vs. rigid, acquisition
  • Shooters: prototyping before committing
  • 3D Printing: hubs, and what not to print
  • CAD: integration, parametric design, weight estimation

docs.title: 3D Printing
docs.text: How we design and print robot parts today.

docs.title: Hubs
docs.text:
• Use a tapered ceiling in printed hubs. Why: makes the hub easier to print. (2026 Off-Season)
  • Put nut access holes on the outside of the tube where possible. (2026 Off-Season)
  • Print high-torque or high-RPM hubs in Onyx or another high-grade engineering material. Why: so the hub survives. (2026 Off-Season)

docs.title: Bearings in Prints
docs.text: • Print tolerance alone won't hold a bearing. See Bearings & Retention.

docs.title: Pulleys
docs.text: • Printed pulleys with print inserts are fine if they stay aligned. See Power Transmission: Pulleys.

docs.title: What Not to Print
docs.text: • Motor standoffs. Use metal; printed standoffs creep. See Structure & Materials.

docs.title: Bearings & Retention
docs.text: How we seat and retain bearings today.

docs.title: Retention
docs.text:
• Retain every bearing positively. Use a bearing hat (retaining plate or flange), shear pins, or another mechanical retainer. Never rely on press fit or print tolerance alone. Why: print tolerance alone didn't hold bearings in, and we had to fall back on epoxy plus spacers on the dead axle setup. (2026 Off-Season)
  • In printed bearing seats, design shear pins into the print. Why: this would have kept the bearings in without the epoxy fix. (2026 Off-Season)
  • Seat bearings in 1/4" plate where weight allows. Why: 1/4" aluminum noticeably improved bearing retention over 1/8". See Structure & Materials. (2026 Off-Season)

docs.title: Alignment
docs.text: • Don't let bearings be the only thing holding a mechanism in alignment. The structure around them has to be rigid. See Power Transmission: Belts.

docs.title: Linear Guide Bearings
docs.text: • See Linear Motion.

docs.title: CAD
docs.text: How we model robots today.

docs.title: Integration ("CAD Hell")
docs.text:
• Get the whole robot fully integrated in CAD early, before fabrication starts. Why: once CAD was finished and parts arrived, the robot came together fast. (2026 Off-Season)
  • How CAD hell fits into the build schedule each year is in that season's plan. See 2027 Season Plan.

docs.title: Parametric Design
docs.text: • Drive the design with variables and constraints so dimensions can change without rebuilding parts. Why: made the CAD dynamic and fast to iterate. (2026 Off-Season)

docs.title: Model What Sticks Out
docs.text: • Model connectors and leave clearance for them, especially RJ45 and USB. Why: they stick out from the device and need clearance. (2026 Off-Season)

docs.title: Weight Estimation
docs.text:
• When every part has a material and fasteners are modeled, expect the real robot to come in under the CAD weight. Don't make parts weaker to cut weight until the estimate says you have to. Why: in past years low-detail CAD meant we came in overweight. In 2026 the detailed CAD turned out conservative, and early weight cutting made parts weaker than they needed to be. (2026 Off-Season)
  • See Structure & Materials: Pocketing.

docs.title: Intakes
docs.text: How we design intakes today.

docs.title: Compliant or Rigid: Pick One
docs.text:
• An intake either flexes and gives on impact, or is rigid enough to stow back. Pick one and commit to it. Why: the original 2026 off-season intake tried to be both and did neither well. (2026 Off-Season)
  • Default to a compliant polycarb design over full metal. Why: cheaper and easier to replace. Switching to polycarb arms with a split-motor design was a great fix. (2026 Off-Season)
  • If the intake is rigid, sync both sides with a jackshaft. Why: it would have kept the rigid version moving together. (2026 Off-Season)

docs.title: Compliance
docs.text: • Use stacked 1/4" polycarbonate as a leaf spring for flex. Why: it flexes very well. (2026 Off-Season)

docs.title: Acquisition
docs.text:
• Go for a big acquisition zone: a cross bar with a 3" diameter roller worked well. (2026 Off-Season)
  • Hold the intake motor with metal plates. Why: it kept the pulleys and belts aligned. (2026 Off-Season)

docs.title: Guidance
docs.text: • Any arm that extends on a rack needs guides on both sides. See Linear Motion.

docs.title: Linear Motion
docs.text: How we guide anything that slides or extends today.

docs.title: Constrain Side to Side
docs.text: • Restrict side-to-side movement on every moving part. The extra friction from guides is worth it. Why: loose belts, rack and pinion drives, and intake arms all failed in 2026 because nothing held them in line. (2026 Off-Season)

docs.title: Rack and Pinion
docs.text:
• Guide both sides of a rack and pinion tightly enough to stay on the rack, especially when it's exposed outside the frame. Constraining one side isn't enough. Why: the exposed intake arm racks needed tight side-to-side control to stay engaged. (2026 Off-Season)
  • Design slider blocks or guides in from the start, not as a fix later. Why: we added them to the intake arms far later than we should have. (2026 Off-Season)

docs.title: Guide Bearings
docs.text: • Don't go smaller than the 2026 off-season guide bearings, and consider going bigger. (2026 Off-Season)

docs.title: Power Transmission
docs.text: How we design belts, pulleys, shafts, and gearing today.

docs.title: Belts
docs.text:
• Belt center-to-center: add about +0.005", not more. Why: +0.010" was meant to reduce friction, but belts ran loose, derailed, and burned pulleys. (2026 Off-Season)
  • Use common, existing belt sizes. Why: avoids supply chain problems and makes spares interchangeable. (2026 Off-Season)
  • Build belt mechanisms rigidly, so alignment doesn't depend on the bearings alone. Center-to-center distance and bearing alignment both have to hold under load. Why: a flexible floor mechanism let load push the belts down, which raised friction until the floor was unusable. (2026 Off-Season)
  • Leave room for the belt to clear itself. Don't package a belt so tightly that it can bind on its own return run. Why: the 2026 floor didn't have the space, and the belt bound on itself. (2026 Off-Season)

docs.title: Pulleys
docs.text:
• Use metal pulleys in high shock-load areas when weight allows. Small metal pulleys are especially robust. Why: they held up extremely well. (2026 Off-Season)
  • Printed pulleys are fine, with print inserts, if they stay aligned. Design for manufacturing and assembly tolerance, not only CAD alignment. Why: the printed pulleys weren't the problem; loose belts and poor real-world alignment derailed belts and burned them. (2026 Off-Season)
  • Buy and design SplineXS pulleys and print inserts, including the metal pulleys, so no adapter is needed. Why: simpler assembly and better torque transmission. (2026 Off-Season)

docs.title: Shafts and Hubs
docs.text:
• SplineXL / MAXSpline works, but avoid it where gear ratios on the hub need to change. Why: the hubs have to be large, which limits ratio changes. (2026 Off-Season)
  • For printed hubs, see 3D Printing.

docs.title: Ratios and Layout
docs.text:
• Calculate gear ratios ahead of time. Don't pick them by feel. (2026 Off-Season)
  • Use as few belt and chain stages as the mechanism allows. Why: simplifying the stages cut friction noticeably compared to the original 2026 robot. (2026 Off-Season)

docs.title: Shooters
docs.text: How we design shooters today.

docs.title: Prototype Before Committing
docs.text: • Prototype and measure compression ourselves before committing to a shooter design. Treat other teams' numbers as a starting point only, and check that their setup matches ours. Why: we set hood compression from other teams' numbers without prototyping. Most of those teams didn't run a full-contact hood, so our compression ended up far higher than needed and hurt shooter performance. (2026 Off-Season)

docs.title: Structure & Materials
docs.text: What we build robots out of today, and how we keep them stiff.

docs.title: Plate
docs.text:
• Use 1/4" aluminum plate over 1/8" when weight allows. Why: much better overall robot rigidity and bearing retention. (2026 Off-Season)
  • McMaster oversized 1/4" aluminum plate is fine to buy. Why: works just as well at a significant cost saving. It isn't as cheap as it used to be, but still saves money. (2026 Off-Season)
  • Tap holes in 1/4" plate instead of adding nuts or extra fasteners. Why: removes fasteners and simplifies integration. (2026 Off-Season)

docs.title: Pocketing
docs.text:
• Don't pocket high-stress areas or surfaces that take external contact. Where you do pocket, keep the ribs substantial. Why: over-pocketing driven by weight worries caused internal and external damage, and we ended up underweight anyway. (2026 Off-Season)
  • Check the weight estimate before pocketing. See CAD: Weight Estimation.

docs.title: Robot Width
docs.text: • A wide robot needs supports perpendicular to the long dimension. Support long shafts and cross bars along their length. Why: a wide robot was great for intake and shooter throughput, but bad for defense and center of gravity. The long lever arm made unsupported shafts flex and long cross bars take a lot of damage. (2026 Off-Season)

docs.title: Standoffs and Mounting
docs.text: • Use metal standoffs for motors, not printed ones. Why: they come in standard sizes and don't creep. (2026 Off-Season)

docs.title: Friction Reduction
docs.text: • Use UHMW tape wherever we need to reduce sliding friction. (2026 Off-Season)

docs.title: Polycarbonate
docs.text:
• For a part that must stay curved, use very thin polycarb (1/32"). Don't rely on thicker polycarb's stiffness to hold a curve. Why: thicker curved pieces didn't keep the shape we needed. (2026 Off-Season)
  • For polycarb as a spring in intakes, see Intakes.

docs.title: Seasons
docs.text:
The record of each season: the plan we went in with, and what we learned.

Season pages are history. The current way we do things lives in the subteam standards, such as Mechanical and Electrical, so you never have to read through past seasons to find today's answer. Each lesson in a retro links to the standard it created or changed.
• Season Plan

• Season Retro
  • Off-Season Retro

docs.title: How a Retro Works
docs.text:
Each year has a Season retro (kickoff through the last event) and an Off-Season retro (the off-season robot, rebuilds, and experiments).

Mark Meaning ✅ Keep Worked well. Became or confirmed a standard. ❌ Fix Hurt us. The standard now says to do it differently. ⚖️ Mixed Real upsides and downsides. The standard says when to use it.

docs.title: End-of-season routine
docs.text:
1. Write the raw notes. A quick list, marked Keep, Fix, or Mixed, with the reason for each.
  2. Update the standards. For each note, add or edit the rule on the matching standards page, with a Why and a link back to this season's retro. If a note reverses an old rule, rewrite the rule; don't add a second one.
  3. Write the retro. Create docs/seasons/<year>/season.md or off-season.md. List each lesson as one line linking to its standard, then keep the raw notes at the bottom under "Original notes."
  4. Add the page to nav in mkdocs.yml and link it from this page.

docs.title: 2026 Off-Season Retro
docs.text: What the 2026 off-season taught us. Each lesson links to the standard where the rule now lives. ✅ Keep · ❌ Fix · ⚖️ Mixed. See Seasons for what each mark means.

docs.title: Top Takeaways
docs.text:
• Constrain anything that moves side to side. Loose belts, rack and pinion drives, and intake arms all failed because nothing held them in line.
  • Tighten belt center-to-center from +0.010" to about +0.005".
  • Don't over-pocket. Detailed CAD overestimated weight, so we cut material we didn't need to and took damage because of it.
  • Get to a fully integrated CAD early. Once CAD was done and parts arrived, the robot came together fast.
  • Prototype before committing, especially for shooter compression.
  • Retain bearings positively with bearing hats or shear pins, not press fit or print tolerance.

docs.title: Power Transmission
docs.text:
• ❌ Belt center-to-center +0.010" was too loose; now +0.005".
  • ✅ Metal pulleys in high shock-load areas, and small pulleys, were very robust.
  • ⚖️ Printed pulleys with inserts were fine; loose belts and misalignment burned them.
  • ❌ Switch to SplineXS pulleys and inserts to drop the adapter.
  • ⚖️ SplineXL / MAXSpline worked, but hubs are too large for adjustable ratios.
  • ✅ Fewer belt and chain stages cut friction.
  • ✅ Gear ratios calculated ahead of time.
  • ✅ Common belt sizes.
  • ❌ Floor belt friction: non-rigid mechanism, belt binding on itself.

docs.title: Structure & Materials
docs.text:
• ✅ 1/4" aluminum plate for rigidity and bearing retention.
  • ✅ McMaster oversized 1/4" plate.
  • ✅ Tapped holes in 1/4" plate.
  • ❌ Over-pocketing in high-stress and contact areas.
  • ⚖️ Wide robot: great throughput, but long lever arm caused flex and damage.
  • ✅ Metal standoffs for motors.
  • ✅ UHMW tape for friction.
  • ❌ Thick polycarb doesn't hold a curve; use 1/32".

docs.title: Bearings & Retention
docs.text:
• ❌ Print tolerance didn't retain bearings; needed epoxy and spacers.
  • ❌ Add bearing hats / positive bearing retention going forward.

docs.title: Linear Motion
docs.text:
• ❌ Rack and pinion needed both sides guided; slider blocks added too late.
  • ❌ Don't go smaller on linear guide bearings.
  • ❌ Restrict side-to-side movement on all moving parts.

docs.title: Intakes
docs.text:
• ⚖️ Original intake tried to be both compliant and rigid; polycarb split-motor redesign worked.
  • ✅ Stacked 1/4" polycarb leaf spring.
  • ✅ Big acquisition: cross bar and 3" roller, motor held by metal plates.

docs.title: Shooters
docs.text: • ❌ No prototype; hood compression copied from teams without full-contact hoods was far too high.

docs.title: 3D Printing
docs.text: • ⚖️ Hubs: tapered ceiling helped; put nut access outside; use Onyx for high torque or RPM.

docs.title: CAD
docs.text:
• ✅ Fully integrated CAD made the build fast.
  • ✅ Parametric design.
  • ⚖️ Detailed CAD came in heavy vs. the real robot, which led to premature weight cutting.
  • ❌ Account for connectors that stick out (RJ45, USB).

docs.title: Connectors
docs.text: • ✅ Molex SL with TPA/CPA held up very well.

docs.title: Power & CAN
docs.text:
• ❌ Mount the PDH-side SB120 to the frame.
  • ❌ Replace breakers after any pop; keep more spares.
  • ❌ Consider the PDH on the CAN loop for current logging.

docs.title: Original Notes
docs.text:
Original notes, as written
  • [-] Belt center to center distance too loose, 0.01 is too much should probably do something like 0.005 going forward, intent was to keep it loose for friction reduction but this definitely backfired
  • [+] 1/4 inch aluminum for improved overall robot rigidity and beating retention, works much better than 1/8" if weight allows
  • [+] Mcmaster oversized 1/4" aluminum plate works just fine despite significant cost reduction (no longer as cheap as it used to be but still good savings)
  • [-] Attention to over pocketing on areas of high stress or external contact, we took a lot of damage both internally and externally. Driven by weight worries but we ended up under weight so this was unnecessary pocketing or the ribs were too small
  • [+/-] Came in way under weight vs CAD, given all parts were assigned materials and fasteners CAD'd it is good that we came in under but also not great because we ended up doing some premature weight optimization that caused parts to be less structurally sound. If we continue to have this fidelity of CAD, consider that the weight tended to come under. Often times we would be overweight because the CAD didn't have enough fidelity, but when it does, it seems like there were some conservatims baked in
  • [+] Metal pulleys in high shock load area and small pulleys proved to be extremely robust, we'll probably opt into should weight allow
  • [+/-] printed pulleys worked fine especially with the print inserts, however due to the loose belts + poor alignment, it would derail and burn the pulleys. I don't think the pulleys themselves were necessary bad but we need to do a better job aligning them (in CAD they were aligned but manufacturing and assembly tolerances exist)
  • [+/-] long robot width was great for throughput for intake and shooter, awful from defense, robot CG, and damage given the long lever arm. Shafts tended to flex when un supported and long cross bars took a lot of damage. Consider more normal to length supports to ensure damage is minimized if we go for a design like this again
  • [-] Linear actuation with rack and pinion, especially with it being exposed outside need to be tightly controlled side to side to stay on the rack. We should have added slider blocks that guide the intake arms way earlier. And you can't assume one side of it is enough, but sides need to be constrained. The trade off for the added friction is 100% worth it
  • [+/-] intake either needs to flex and give, or rigid enough to stow back on impact. Initial design took both concepts and poorly implemented both. A jack shaft that synchronized the movement would have helped for the rigid design, though replacing with polycarb arms with the split motor design ended up being a great adaption. For cost the replaceability, I'd probably bias towards polycarb compliant design in the future instead of full metal
  • [+] Big acquisition + rigid intake, having the cross bar and 3" diameter roller was a good design, additionally the metal plates actually holding the motor ensured that the pulleys and belts stayed aligned
  • [-] bearing retention need something more than just print tolerance, we ended up doing a combination of expoy + spaces for the dead axle setup but it would have been better if we had some shear pins in the print to make sure that the bearings stay in
  • [+/-] hub design with the tapered ceiling helped printing, definitely put the nut access holes to be on the outside of the tube if possible. Almost always use onyx or high grade engineering prints to ensure that the hub survives if used in high torque or high rpm setup
  • [-] potentially consider using bigger bearings for guiding the linear rail, I would probably not go any smaller than what we used this year
  • [+] Leaf spring effect of the stacked quarter inch polycarb is really good for flex, we should continue using this in future intake designs
  • [+] Simplified mechanisms for reduced friction from belt chains, definitely better than the original 2026 bot I'm this instance
  • [-] relying on rigidity from polycarb for curved pieces is not great if you actually need the curvature to exist, go for very thin (1/32") if you need something curved
  • [+] When CAD is finished and parts are here, the robot was completed relatively fast. We should bring back CAD hell and have a completely integrated system in CAD early
  • [-] no prototype/misinformed from the season ended up completely harming shooter performance, too much compression the hood, informed from other teams but given them most teams didn't do a full contact good, our compression ended up being significantly more than what was needed
  • [+] Uhwm tape is great for reducing friction, recommend for all future friction reduction usage
  • [-] we should use the spline xs pulley/print inserts so we don't have to use an adapter. Simplifies assembly and better torque transmission, along with metal pulleys we should buy the spline xs version as well
  • [+] Parametric design utilizing variables and contrains allowed for dynamic CAD and fast iteration, we should continue doing this
  • [-] friction in the floor made it unusable, two factors, one of which was already known but if the belts are pushed down by load then the friction increases, especially since we actually had not enough space to remove binding of the belt on top of itself, the mechanical design implementation lacked rigidy at the end and the alignment of the mechanisms relied on the bearing alignment but next time we should ensure that the mechanism are rigidly constructed with minimal flex to ensure belt center to center distance and bearing are all aligned correctly
  • [+/-] spline xl/max spline was overall successful though given how big the hubs need to be, I won't really suggest using this if we need to adjust gear ratios on the hub
  • [+] Actual calculation of gear ratios ahead of time definitely something we should be doing
  • [+] Using common or existing belt sizes to reduce supply chain issues
  • [+] Incorpating tapped holes in quarter inch plates to remove fasteners and integration
  • [+] Metal standoffs, they come in standard size and work great for motors, we should use these instead of printed ones since they don't creep
  • [-] account for connectors, especially things like rj45 and USB where they stick out
  • [+] TPA/CPA molec SL has held up incredibly well
  • [-] mount PDH side SB120 onto the frame somewhere
  • [-] breaker needs to replaced after any pop, we should also have many more of those
  • [-] consider adding PDH in the CAN loop for current logging
  • [-] in general if there are any moving parts, restrict side to side movement
  • [-] bearing hat/bearing retention, need to do in the future

docs.text: How TorBots plans to design, build, and compete in 2027, based on where the team stands as of November 2026. It applies the team-wide Robot Design Philosophy to this season's people, space, and budget.

docs.text:
The original presentation is embedded below. Click it, then use the arrow keys or the on-screen buttons to move between slides, or open the deck full screen.

The rest of this page has the same content as text, so it can be searched and linked to.

Scope

This plan is set by our current constraints. We'll revisit it each season as people, space, and budget change.

How mentors and students rate on FRC robot work specifically:

Area Mentors Students Strategic design Strength Neutral Autonomous & software Strength Weakness Mechanical design Weakness Weakness Manufacturing & assembly Weakness Strength Electrical Strength Strength

  • Software and manufacturing each have one strong group, on opposite sides.

docs.title: Constraints
docs.text:
Resource limits that apply to the whole team:

Resource Status Impact Shop space Limited Not enough room to practice driving well for teleop. Budget Limited Caps what we can buy for parts, mechanisms, and spares. Manpower Limited Limited students and mentors. Shop hours are capped by how many mentors are available to supervise. Manufacturing tolerance Limited Parts we make in-house can only hold so tight a tolerance.

docs.title: Autonomous Drives Matches
docs.text:
Since 2022, the alliance that wins auto has won the match about 4 times in 5.

  • 77.9% auto winner's match win rate across all 77,997 decided matches, 2022–2026.
  • Quals 78.6%, playoffs 74.6%.
  • Every season since 2022 sits between 76% and 79% overall.

Official events only. Matches tied in auto or final score are excluded. Data: The Blue Alliance.

docs.title: Built Around Autonomous
docs.text:
FRC matches are shaped by autonomous, and our team is set up to deliver on it.

Mentors bring depth in strategy and autonomous software. Students bring strength in manufacturing and assembly, so we can build, repair, and deliver the robots autonomous testing depends on. Together we design a robot built for its auto paths, deliver the prototype and final robots as early as possible, and test autos on an accurate field in our own shop.

This is built on:

  • Mentor depth in strategy and autonomous software.
  • Student strength in manufacturing and assembly.
  • Auto outcomes carrying into the rest of the match.
  • Auto testing that fits the shop space we have.

docs.title: How We Deliver It
docs.text:
• The robot: built for auto paths. Mechanism layout is chosen around the autonomous routine. Intake and shooter, or intake and end effector, face the directions that make auto paths shortest and cleanest.
  • The schedule: robots early. Deliver a software-testable prototype early, then the final robot as early as possible, for weeks of software work and auto tuning. Mechanical focuses on 1–1.5 mechanisms' worth of robot, so the team ships a simple robot that can be tested for a long time.
  • The field: accurate shop field. Build high-quality, accurate field elements sized to fit our shop, so autonomous is tested as close to the real field as possible.

docs.title: One Elite Mechanism
docs.text:
We focus on 1–1.5 mechanisms' worth of robot. We deliver one elite mechanism, and that mechanism handles and delivers the autonomous performance we're after.

  • We have traditionally not had success focusing on multiple mechanisms at once.
  • More can be added later. We leave room for upgrades throughout the season.

Rule

Complex enough to enable software. Simple enough to deliver on time.

docs.title: Before Kickoff
docs.text:
Get the shop ready for vision and auto work before the game is revealed on Jan 9. All four items get done across two work days: Sat Nov 14 and Sat Dec 12.

  • Working drive base: a drive base that runs, ready for software and auto work.
  • Protocube running: the protocube is up and running for prototyping.
  • Strip current robot: strip the current robot down to what vision work needs.
  • Clear field elements: take down the field elements except the trench, to open space for vision.

docs.title: Kickoff and Kitbot
docs.text:
Get hands on game pieces and a driving robot as fast as possible.

  • 1–2 hour game breakdown. We compress the day-one game breakdown to 1–2 hours, down from our traditional multi-hour session. The time we save goes straight into prototyping and studying how the robot interacts with game pieces.
  • Kitbot on swerve (pending kitbot review). If the 2027 kitbot design looks promising, we build it on a swerve drivetrain over kickoff weekend. Students bring up a working robot that bootstraps prototyping, and the team gains a second robot to use throughout the season as needed.

docs.title: Alpha Bot and CAD Hell
docs.text:
Prove the geometry on a driving robot, then release CAD that fabrication can trust.

  • Week 2: Alpha bot. A robot that is accurate in geometry and materials, without most of the moving parts. It drives, with some actuation, so we can confirm how the robot interacts with the field and game pieces before committing to the final design. Some prototyping can bleed over into this week; what it teaches us can still inform the CAD.
  • Week 3: CAD hell. Moving parts and packaging get worked out until the CAD is high fidelity. Releasing high-fidelity CAD lets fabrication and assembly stay focused, which plays to the students' strength in manufacturing and assembly.

docs.title: Six-Week Build Schedule
docs.text:
The timeline is aggressive on purpose, with a one-week buffer and software testing the whole way.

Phase Dates Focus Kickoff weekend Jan 9–10 Kitbot. Kitbot on swerve, built over the first weekend. Week 1 Jan 11–17 Prototyping. Mechanisms and game piece interaction worked out, with the kitbot as a starting point. Week 2 Jan 18–24 Alpha bot. Confirms geometry and material choices. Mostly wood and static parts. Some prototyping bleeds over. Week 3 Jan 25–31 CAD hell. Moving parts and packaging for the final robot. Week 4 Feb 1–7 Fabrication. Design released to fab; parts start. Week 5 Feb 8–14 Assembly & wiring. Final robot built and wired. Week 6 Feb 15–21 Final bot. Final robot delivered. Can slip up to 1 week. Week 6+ Feb 22 on Tuning. Auto and software tuning, mechanical fixes as they come up. Runs into the competition season.
  • Field: main field elements are done before the alpha bot. Mentor-led, with students as bandwidth allows.
  • Software: tests continuously on the alpha bot to learn what software needs, and feeds that back into the design.

1-week buffer

The schedule can slip by one week if needed for:

  • WCP's week 2 concept bot release, as a reference for more prototyping before the alpha bot.
  • CAD hell not progressing fast enough.
  • Manufacturing or supply chain delays.

docs.title: Competition Season
docs.text:
Tuning continues between events, with one optional window to install an upgrade mechanism.

When Dates Event Status After week 6 Feb 22 – Mar 18 Tuning. Auto and software tuning, mechanical fixes. Driver practice ramps up. Comp week 3 Mar 19–21 CA District Los Angeles Event, El Segundo Attending Option A Mar 22 – Apr 1 Upgrade window after LA Optional Comp week 5 Apr 2–4 CA District Hueneme Port Event, Port Hueneme Attending Option B Apr 5–14 Upgrade window after Hueneme Optional Comp week 7 Apr 15–18 FIRST California Southern State Championship (DCMP), Anaheim If points qualify Championship Apr 28 – May 1 FIRST Championship (Worlds), Houston If we qualify

An upgrade mechanism is optional. If we add one, it goes in after either LA or Hueneme, not both.

docs.title: Shop Hours
docs.text:
28 hours a week to start, set by mentor availability. Hours are flexible, and we add more as needed.

Day Hours Time Mon 5 h 3:30–8:30 PM Tue — Possible swap later Wed 5 h 3:30–8:30 PM Thu — Possible swap later Fri 5 h 3:30–8:30 PM Sat 8 h 10 AM–6 PM Sun 5 h 1–6 PM

Sunday first. Early in the season, Sunday gives us mentor support while we're designing. Later, if it's more productive for students doing manufacturing and assembly, we can trade Sunday for a Tuesday or Thursday.

docs.title: Consistency Is the Game
docs.text:
A TorBots robot wins on consistency. We go for a consistent autonomous, and that usually means a highly automated teleop robot too. The robot is built to do the same thing well every match.

Driver practice:

  • Is built around consistency, not peak performance.
  • Ramps up as auto and software get tuned and competition gets closer.
  • Without a full practice field, we don't plan on an explosive driver performance.

docs.title: Alliance Selection
docs.text:
A consistent robot needs partners who can raise the ceiling.

  • Default pick: consistent + high upside. Pick higher-upside, riskier teams. Our consistency sets the floor, and their variance gives the alliance a real chance to win the event.
  • Default to avoid: consistent + consistent. We don't play in a high-variance way that can turn a match on our own, so pairing with another consistent team caps how high the alliance can go. Exception: if a consistent partner is enough to win the event, take it.

Scouting

Scout and build pick lists with this in mind: look for each team's ceiling and upside, not only its average.

docs.title: Season Goals
docs.text:
TorBots sets two goals each season, in order:

  • Threshold goal: qualify for the Southern California District Championship (DCMP).
  • Objective goal: qualify for the FIRST Championship (Worlds).

The threshold goal is the minimum bar for a successful season. The objective goal is the stretch target — worth pushing for, but not at the cost of missing DCMP.

docs.title: Design for the Whole Team
docs.text:
A good robot design isn't just one that could theoretically score a lot of points. It's one this team can actually build, wire, program, and keep running all season.

That means designing around students and mentors together, not students alone. If any part of the team can't sustain a mechanism — not enough students, not enough experience, not enough mentor time — it's the wrong choice, no matter how good it looks on paper.

Design for the team we have this year, not the team we had two years ago or the team we wish we had.

docs.title: Student and Mentor Capacity Are Real Constraints
docs.text:
A mechanism only works if the students building it have the numbers and experience to pull it off, not just the potential to learn it eventually. One student who understands a mechanism, with no one else backing them up, is a risk — if they're out sick or graduate, that knowledge is gone. Aim for designs the whole subteam can own, not just its strongest member.

The same goes for mentors. Even if students can build something, if the mentors backing them don't have the time or expertise to support it, it's not going to work. Mentor support is a real constraint, same as budget, timeline, or shop access.

Neither side covers for the other. A strong student group with thin mentor support is just as risky as strong mentors trying to carry a thin student group.

docs.title: In Practice
docs.text:
Before committing to a mechanism, ask:

  • Can our current students build and maintain this reliably, not just in theory?
  • Does that knowledge live with one or two people, or is it spread across the subteam?
  • Do the mentors involved have the time and expertise to support this through build and competition?
  • If it breaks at competition, can we fix it, or does it depend on one person who might not be there?
  • Is the upside toward Worlds worth risking DCMP?

When in doubt, pick the mechanism the team already understands well over a new one you'd be learning under competition pressure, unless you genuinely have the student depth and mentor support to take it on.

For how this applies to the current season, see the 2027 Season Plan.
